text:
Peter Naur in 1985 wrote that programming is the act of building a working theory of the system in our minds, and this often takes form as tacit knowledge in the head of programmers. Even if you handed the complete codebase and perfect documentation to a completely new team, they would often need to go back to the old team and ask questions.
And before agents, we often built this working theory of the system by writing the code by hand. It helps us figure out the "grain" of the codebase so we have a better idea of how to extend it.
So what happens when agents are writing the code? The main avenue with which we built the working theory of the system in our mind is now taken away, and we're left feeling like our understanding of the system is blinded.
I ended up more or less changing my entire workflow. Four main principles:
1. Interrogation/interview-based design and specification
2. Make the decisions that matter and leave the rest to the agent.
3. Use agent to generate explainers, quizzes, and simulations.
4. Use verifiers and guardrails in the coding loop.
Interview-based design and spec
When I tell the agent what I want to build or extend, there's naturally ambiguity. But the agent knows what is ambiguous to it, so it can ask me. /grill-me is one way to do this. You'd think this would be commonplace now, but it's actually not. Some people are still wondering why they're getting bad results. It's because they're not resolving the ambiguity.
Making the decisions that matter
Not every decision matters in a product. Agents are fast at writing code and pretty good at some of the nitty gritty details, so I let it make those decisions. Also, if a particular subsystem is commonplace and undifferentiating, such as login, then I also let it make architectural decisions for that subsystem.
For decisions that are product differentiators, where that differentiation is supported by technology, I make decisions on the stack, the architecture, and the approach. This is the design phase. Because agents tend to make the mainstream decisions, they almost always take a midwit approach which doesn't leverage the technology in a way that makes a difference for the customer.
Some try to build this understanding from code reviews. I personally don't think it's the way to go, because it's not motivating. I find that I'm more motivated to learn how the system works today, because I want to change how it works tomorrow--and it sticks in my head better too (no different than pre-agents).
Generating explainers, quizzes, and simulations
As I'm doing design for an improvement and I don't know how a part of the system works, I can ask questions of the agent in chat. If I still don't get it, I can ask for diagrams (either ASCII or mermaid). But if it's an entire subsystem, I have a skill in which I can ask for visual and interactive explainers. It'll generate a markdown page (or html) that has these interactive components that help demonstrate a concept.
To help make the concept stick, there are quizzes after each section and at the end.
With the computational simulations, I generate a throwaway tool in which I can explore the state space. This doesn't happen as often, as I try to keep state spaces small, and for those explainers tend to work well.
With the design simulations, a same-model agent and a cross-model agent and I will talk about an explainer, and we'll name things that we understand or notice about the design and the intended direction we want to extend it. Then, we'll use subagents to generate options and then discuss the pros and cons. I find this is a good way for me to understand the dead-ends of a design.
Using Verifiers and Guardrails
I define guardrails as mechanistic checks that doesn't change with the feature. such as linters, typecheckers, and pre-commit hooks are all guardrails. Verifiers are mechanistic checks that will be different with each feature, such as unit/integration tests.
For more complicated states or concurrent parts, I'll ask the agent to use formal methods to write a proof. Then use the proof to generate a trace (a series of steps that demonstrate a happy or unhappy path). Then I run that trace in unit tests (kinda like property-based testing--so I guess this can be called trace-based testing), and the code has to adhere to the trace.
I also wrote a design verifier, where the requirements in the spec can be converted into a series of mechanically checkable rules. Then during testing, the verifier fires up the headless browser and uses the DOM measurements of the page to see if it matches up to the rules. This was completely impractical before agents.
All of this so a) I can be sure that the agent is doing what it's supposed to with the decisions that it's making b) I can be out of the coding loop, so that I'm not up at 2am begging, "you fixed this, but you broke that. pls fix." The agent can check for itself.
---
If any of this sounds helpful, lemme know. I've been wondering if other engineers care about understanding the code that's being written, or if people just don't care anymore. I've spoken to a few, and it seems to be split. And it may just be a matter of degree and detail. Some like it at a higher level. Some like it nitty gritty.

The short lifespans are to encourage people to actually automate, not just say they want to.
If the cert lifetime is 5 years, Bill installs "just the first one" manually, solemnly swearing they will automate next time, and in five years nobody even knows who Bill was, Bill left three years ago. How do we replace the certificate?
If the cert lifetime is 2 years. Bill is still there or maybe somebody on the team still knows Bill's email address, but most likely the decision is taken to "just do it manually once because it's urgent" and we just recurse. This would have been the "obvious" choice when ISRG lit up Let's Encrypt.
But because the cert lifetime was 90 days, Bill gets told it's expiring at about the same time he's about to shove that "Actually automate certificates" work onto the back burner. Oh yeah, right, we should actually do that.
Now, it may be that at a startup that "Automation" is initially "Put it on Natalie the intern's TODO list every Monday" but by week six Natalie has learned about cron, or Windows event scheduling, or a dozen other ways to make stuff you always do regularly happen without actual work. Today I expect her LLM will tell her how to do it.
And Natalie is going to discover that some "permanent" solutions are more permanent than others, that you want monitoring and so on. But because Let's Encrypt is so popular unless you're doing something pretty esoteric you won't even be the first person to ask about it this month.

text:
(Apologies if I'm misreading your reply. I'm assuming it was sarcasm but Poe's Law might apply here.)
This does feel a lot like the "Agile era" that was the last silver bullet that was supposed to fix software development forever and the "Cloud era" that was supposed to fix infrastructure and deployments.
Agile had a few good ideas. Code reviews and automated tests are commonly used today.
It had a few plausible ideas that it took too far. We are better at recognising the value of incremental development over big up-front design today - despite the ironic clash this seems to be having with agentic workflows - but almost everyone hates stand-ups and lots of projects have gone off the rails by breaking things down far too much and never committing to anything and so never getting anywhere.
And it had plenty of ideas that almost all of us have thrown out as unpleasant and/or unworkable. Pair programming comes to mind immediately.
What didn't really change was the fundamental nature of software development. Did we adopt a few useful ideas and get a more more efficient and improve quality a bit? Certainly. Did we get orders of magnitude better at anything and give up all the tried and tested ways of working in favour of radical new ones that never quite felt right? No.
On our current trajectory I'm expecting a broadly similar outcome for LLMs. They're now very good at some things. But they are still pretty bad at other things that also matter - and some of the reasons they are bad at them are an inherent part of how they work and therefore probably can't be overcome (at least not with incremental improvements on the technology that still basically work the same way). So I am expecting to see a period of consolidation with a lot of organisations pulling back from their dramatic leaps into the unknown and downsizing of dev teams once the big AI companies start squeezing financially and the problems of developer burnout and stagnating skills and low morale that we're already seeing after just a few months become endemic. And then as I suggested in another comment I think it's also increasingly possible that we'll see developers unionise and/or push for professional regulation and licensing so they can resist the pressure to just ship whatever their agent wrote without even bothering to check it but still being responsible when inevitably things then go wrong.
